strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: generating compositional, physically plausible 3D object pairs/scenes rather than isolated monolithic assets. This is relevant to 3D generation, embodied AI, and simulation data creation.

The proposed training-free pipeline is practical and reasonably motivated: it uses 2D/3D generative priors for spatial guidance, preserves high-quality individual meshes, and then performs registration plus SDF-based collision-aware refinement.

The generate-then-compose framing is a sensible alternative to directly segmenting fused generated scenes, and the qualitative comparisons show clear cases where direct PartField segmentation produces holes or where naive registration gives poor poses.

The paper includes several useful components beyond the main alignment stage, including a global-to-local registration strategy, collision loss, multi-object sequential composition, and a VLM-based repair loop for difficult occlusion cases.

The claimed dataset of roughly 8,300 compositional scenes with individual assets and poses could be a useful resource if released with sufficient metadata, generation prompts, licenses, and quality annotations.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is too limited for the strength of the claims. Quantitative evaluation is reported on only 10 test cases, which is far too small to establish robustness across object categories, occlusion patterns, multi-object scenes, or failure modes.

There is no convincing ablation study. The paper does not isolate the contributions of OBB scaling, GeoTransformer, scale-aware ICP, the SDF term, the beta schedule, anchor selection, or the VLM refinement loop, so it is difficult to know which parts are essential and how sensitive the method is.

The method depends heavily on closed or external systems such as Nano Banana Pro/Gemini, TRELLIS2, Hunyuan3D, GeoTransformer, and PartField. This raises reproducibility concerns, especially because prompt details, stochastic generation settings, API/model versions, failure filtering, and computational cost are not sufficiently specified.

The quantitative metrics are incomplete. CLIP scores over rendered views are a weak proxy for 3D compositional correctness, and intersection ratios measure only one aspect of physical plausibility. The paper does not evaluate support/contact validity, stability under simulation, affordance usefulness, orientation correctness, or human preference/quality judgments.

The baseline comparison is not fully satisfying. Jigsaw and 2BY2 are not designed for this exact text/image-guided generated-object setting, while PartField+RANSAC is a relatively simple classical baseline. Stronger comparisons or carefully adapted baselines for object-object placement and VLM/geometric composition would make the case more convincing.

The dataset contribution is under-described. The manuscript states that 8,300 scenes will be released, but provides little information on category coverage, prompt construction, quality control, train/test splits, licensing of generated and source assets, filtering criteria, annotation format, or rates of invalid scenes.

The VLM-based agentic optimization is promising but insufficiently formalized and evaluated. It is unclear how many cases require it, how often it succeeds, how the stopping criterion is applied, whether the VLM sees privileged cross-sections, and whether the process is stable or reproducible.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence. Terms such as 'physically-sound', 'strict physical plausibility', and suitability for robot simulation are not supported by dynamics tests, contact simulation, mass/friction/material annotation, or downstream manipulation experiments.

The method inherits limitations from 2D guidance and mesh reconstruction; the paper acknowledges some failures with symmetry and heavy occlusion, but does not quantify failure rates or provide systematic analysis across object topology and interaction type.

Presentation quality is uneven, with repeated typos and wording issues such as 'collsion', 'occulsion', and 'overlop', and some equations/details are underspecified, for example the exact correspondence update, SDF discretization/resolution, optimization variables, sampling strategy, and handling of non-watertight meshes.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: generating interactive/compositional 3D assets with object-object spatial relationships, which is relevant to simulation, robotics, and 3D content creation.

The generate-then-compose framing is intuitive and practically motivated: using a scene-level 3D generation as spatial guidance while preserving separate high-quality object meshes addresses a real weakness of monolithic 3D generation and direct part segmentation.

The proposed pipeline combines several reasonable components: global-to-local registration, scale-aware ICP, SDF-based collision penalties, and VLM-guided refinement for cases where rigid transformations cannot fix geometry mismatches.
The qualitative figures are useful and show some plausible examples where the method appears to improve over direct segmentation and simple registration baselines.
The claimed 8.3k compositional-scene dataset could be valuable if released with sufficient metadata, licensing clarity, quality control, and evaluation protocols.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is far too limited for the strength of the claims. The main quantitative evaluation uses only 10 test cases, which is inadequate for a paper claiming robust, scalable, collision-aware 3D compositional generation across daily objects and multi-part scenes.

The method is mostly a pipeline assembled from existing proprietary or external systems: Nano Banana Pro/Gemini, TRELLIS2/Hunyuan3D, PartField, GeoTransformer, ICP, and SDF optimization. The paper does not make a convincing case that the algorithmic contribution is sufficiently original beyond system integration.

Reproducibility is a major concern. Key components are closed or vaguely specified, including Nano Banana Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, prompts, image editing behavior, VLM feedback format, stopping criteria, and implementation details. The manuscript even leaves the code-release sentence incomplete.

The baselines are weak and not fully appropriate. Jigsaw is designed for fractured-object assembly, 2BY2 is retrained from scratch without sufficient details, and PartField+RANSAC is a very limited classical baseline. Stronger or more directly relevant 3D composition/editing baselines and ablations are missing.

There are no meaningful ablations isolating the contribution of the proposed components: OBB scaling, GeoTransformer initialization, ICP, SDF collision loss, beta schedule, and agentic refinement. As written, it is unclear which parts actually matter.

The physical-plausibility claim is overstated. The method optimizes collision/intersection terms but does not model stability, support, contact realism, gravity, mass, friction, affordances, or simulator validity. Calling the outputs physically sound or interactive is not adequately supported.

The quantitative metrics are insufficient. CLIP similarity against prompts or generated images is a weak proxy for compositional correctness, and collision rates alone do not capture whether object-object relationships are semantically or physically valid. No human evaluation or task-based robotics/simulation evaluation is provided.

The dataset contribution is under-specified. The paper gives only aggregate counts and broad descriptions, with little detail about generation prompts, category distribution, filtering, quality annotation, licensing/attribution of generated and user-provided meshes, train/test splits, or failure rates.

The VLM-based agentic optimization is vague and potentially brittle. The paper shows a few examples but does not quantify how often it is invoked, how many iterations are needed, success/failure rates, cost, latency, or whether the VLM feedback is deterministic and reproducible.

Several method details are unclear or technically shaky: the SDF loss appears to sample vertices rather than surfaces, the optimization variables and constraints on rotation/scale are not fully specified, correspondences in Eq. 3 are underspecified, and the manuscript contains formula/typographical errors that make implementation ambiguous.

The paper’s writing and presentation have many errors and overclaims, including repeated misspellings, awkward terminology, inconsistent notation, and unsupported statements such as consistently yielding strict physical plausibility from any viewpoint.

The limitations section acknowledges some failures, but the acknowledged dependence on 2D priors and occlusion ambiguity directly undermines the central claim of robust 3D compositional reasoning. These are not minor edge cases for the proposed problem setting.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: generating interactive 3D object compositions with independent assets and physically plausible object-object relationships, rather than fused monolithic meshes. This is well motivated for simulation, robotics, and scalable 3D content creation.

The proposed training-free pipeline is conceptually appealing. It combines strong 2D/3D generative priors with PartField-based spatial guidance, global-to-local registration, SDF-based collision penalties, and VLM-driven corrective refinement. While many pieces are borrowed, the integration is coherent and targets a clear gap in current 3D generation workflows.

The qualitative results are strong and communicate the method's advantages clearly, especially compared with direct scene segmentation and registration-only baselines. The multi-view examples and multi-object extensions make the output quality and intended use case easy to understand.

The reported quantitative results, though limited, support the main claims: Interact3D improves CLIP-based semantic consistency and substantially reduces surface and volume intersection rates relative to Jigsaw, 2BY2, and PartField+RANSAC on the evaluated cases.

The planned release of an approximately 8,300-scene interactive 3D dataset is a meaningful contribution. Even if the method itself is largely a pipeline, such data could be valuable for future work on compositional 3D generation and robot simulation.

The paper is generally clear, with a readable problem formulation, explicit pipeline stages, and useful failure-case discussion. The authors acknowledge important limitations around fine-grained joints, heavy occlusion, and reliance on 2D spatial priors.
weaknesses: The experimental validation is quite small relative to the breadth of the claims. The main quantitative evaluation uses only 10 test cases, which is insufficient to convincingly establish generality across object categories, interaction types, occlusion patterns, and multi-object scenes.

There is no ablation study isolating the contributions of the main components, such as GeoTransformer vs. ICP/RANSAC, SDF optimization, anchor selection, the beta schedule, or the VLM agentic refinement loop. This makes it hard to judge which parts are essential and how robust the pipeline is.

Reproducibility is a concern because the method relies heavily on proprietary or rapidly changing external systems such as Nano Banana Pro/Gemini and TRELLIS2/Hunyuan services. Prompt sensitivity, API versions, failure rates, runtime, and cost are not sufficiently characterized.

The dataset contribution is promising but underspecified. The paper gives the scale and broad composition statistics, but lacks enough detail on generation protocol, quality filtering, licenses/attribution of generated and source assets, train/test splits, metadata schema, and failure/acceptance criteria.

The method's novelty is more systems-level than algorithmic. The SDF collision loss, point-cloud registration, image editing loop, and VLM feedback are reasonable, but individually standard. The paper would benefit from positioning itself more explicitly as an applied/systems contribution rather than implying a fundamentally new generative model.

The evaluation metrics only partially capture the claimed physical plausibility. Surface/volume intersection rates measure collision, but not stability, support, affordance correctness, contact realism, or usability in an actual physics simulator or robot-learning pipeline.

The VLM-based agentic refinement is described mostly qualitatively. There are no statistics on success rate, number of iterations, cases where refinement degrades geometry, or comparison against non-agentic prompt/edit variants.

Some baseline choices are imperfect. Jigsaw and 2BY2 are not designed for exactly this generative setting, and the paper does not compare with stronger practical pipelines that may combine modern 3D generation, segmentation, and optimization. The absence of released 2BY2 weights also introduces uncertainty in the fairness of that comparison.

The manuscript has several writing and presentation issues, including repeated typos such as 'collsion', 'occulsion', and 'overlop', and some incomplete phrasing around code release. These do not undermine the core contribution but should be fixed for publication quality.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and important problem: generating compositional, interactive 3D object scenes while preserving individual asset quality and object-object relationships, which is relevant for simulation and robotics data generation.

The proposed generate-then-compose framing is practically appealing. Using a generated 3D scene as spatial guidance while composing higher-quality individual meshes is a sensible way to avoid the fused-geometry artifacts of direct 3D scene generation.

The pipeline combines several complementary components: global-to-local registration, SDF-based collision penalties, and a VLM-driven refinement loop for cases where rigid pose correction is insufficient.

The paper includes useful qualitative examples, multi-view renderings, failure cases, and ablations showing that GeoTransformer+ICP, SDF optimization, and agentic refinement each improve the reported metrics.
The claimed dataset of approximately 8,300 compositional 3D scenes could be valuable if released with clear metadata, licenses, generation settings, and quality annotations.
weaknesses: The central novelty is somewhat limited: the method is mostly a pipeline built from existing proprietary or external systems, including Nano Banana Pro, TRELLIS2, PartField, GeoTransformer, Gemini/Qwen-style VLMs, and SDF pose optimization. The paper would be stronger with a clearer statement of what is algorithmically new beyond system integration.

Reproducibility is a major concern. Key components are proprietary, underspecified, or cited only as web services/future systems; prompts, seeds, model versions, rendering settings, human-rating protocol, VLM prompts, and dataset construction details are not sufficiently specified. The code/dataset availability line is incomplete.

The evaluation evidence is not fully convincing. The quantitative test set has only 150 cases, appears closely tied to the authors' own generation pipeline, and lacks ground-truth poses or task-level validation in simulation/robotics. CLIP and VLM scores are weak proxies for 3D object-object relationship correctness.

The comparison to baselines may be unfair or not fully diagnostic. Several baselines were not designed for this exact setting, lack access to the same text/image guidance, or cannot optimize scale; this makes the large performance gap less conclusive about the proposed components.

The physical-plausibility claims are overstated. The metrics measure mesh interpenetration, but do not establish stability, support/contact correctness, gravity consistency, dynamics, material properties, affordances, or actual usability in a simulator. The text sometimes claims physically sound or guaranteed plausibility beyond the evidence.

The agentic refinement loop is under-specified and hard to assess scientifically. It depends on VLM judgment and image-editing behavior, but the stopping criteria, failure rate, prompt generation format, cost/runtime, and robustness across model choices are unclear.

The dataset contribution is promising but insufficiently validated. The manuscript does not provide detailed quality statistics, annotation schema, train/test splits, license/attribution treatment for generated and source assets, or independent inspection of dataset errors.

Some claims are too strong relative to the shown failures. The appendix reports failures from symmetry, mesh holes, and collision-induced divergence, and the method remains dependent on 2D priors that can propagate occlusion-induced errors into 3D composition.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and relevant problem: composing independently usable 3D assets into interactive scenes with plausible object-object relationships, rather than producing monolithic fused meshes.

The generate-then-compose idea is practically motivated, and the pipeline combines reasonable components: image-guided 3D generation, PartField-based spatial guidance, global-to-local registration, SDF-based collision penalties, and VLM-guided refinement.

The paper includes qualitative examples, ablations, and explicit failure cases, and the proposed dataset of roughly 8,300 generated interactive scenes could be useful if released with sufficient metadata and validation.
weaknesses: The main contribution is largely an engineering pipeline assembled from existing proprietary or external systems rather than a technically novel method. Nano Banana Pro, Gemini, TRELLIS2, GeoTransformer, PartField, CLIP, and Qwen3 carry much of the capability, while the paper's own algorithmic additions are relatively standard registration and SDF collision optimization.

Reproducibility is a major concern. Several key dependencies are proprietary or underspecified, prompts and implementation details are incomplete, and the claimed code/dataset release is only promised. This makes it difficult to independently verify the results or reproduce the dataset.

The experimental evidence is not convincing enough for the claims. Evaluation uses only 150 test cases, with unclear sampling, no train/test provenance for generated data, and no detailed human-study protocol such as number of raters, instructions, inter-rater agreement, or statistical significance.

The baselines are not fully satisfactory. Jigsaw and 2BY2 are not designed for this exact image/text-guided compositional generation setting, MIDI is trained for a different distribution, and PartField+RANSAC is a weak classical baseline. Stronger comparisons to recent object-object alignment or commercial/interactive 3D generation systems are missing.

The metrics only partially measure the stated goal. CLIP and VLM ratings are weak proxies for 3D compositional correctness, while the intersection ratios capture penetration but not support, stability, contact realism, scale plausibility, affordances, articulation, or actual usability in robotic simulation. Thus the repeated claims of 'physically sound' or 'interactive' scenes are overstated.

The agentic refinement loop is especially under-evaluated. The paper shows examples and an ablation, but does not report success rate, number of iterations, failure modes, cost, latency, prompt sensitivity, or whether the VLM/image editor can introduce new artifacts or semantic drift.

The dataset contribution is insufficiently substantiated. The manuscript says the dataset contains over 8,000 scenes, but does not provide rigorous quality control, annotation schema details, licensing/attribution discussion for generated assets, physical validation, or comparison with existing datasets beyond scale.

The paper's claims sometimes exceed the demonstrated evidence. Collision-aware placement is not the same as physically valid interaction, and qualitative figures do not establish that the scenes are suitable for simulation or robot learning.

Clarity is acceptable at a high level, but important operational details are missing: how PartField segments are matched to objects, how SDFs are computed for noisy generated meshes, optimization parameterization and convergence criteria, multi-object ordering effects, and exact prompts/settings for all generative models.

strengths: Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the paper is best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution with a dataset component. Under that framing, the work is compelling: it tackles a timely and practically important problem in compositional 3D generation, namely producing independent interactive assets with plausible object-object relationships rather than fused scene meshes.

The core system design is sensible and well motivated. Using a generated 3D scene as spatial guidance while preserving high-quality separately generated assets is a strong idea, and the two-stage pipeline of robust registration followed by SDF-based collision-aware refinement directly addresses common failure modes in 3D compositional generation.

The paper provides substantial qualitative evidence. The examples show meaningful improvements over direct PartField segmentation, feed-forward assembly baselines, and classical registration, especially in preserving mesh quality and reducing visible interpenetration.

The quantitative results support the main claims: Interact3D improves text/image CLIP scores, human and VLM ratings, and both surface and volume intersection rates on 150 test cases. The ablation study is useful and shows that GeoTransformer-based alignment, SDF refinement, and the agentic loop each contribute.

The proposed dataset of about 8,300 compositional 3D scenes, including individual assets and poses, could be valuable for future work if released with sufficient metadata, validation, and licensing clarity.

The paper is generally clear, with helpful diagrams and failure case analysis. The limitations around symmetry, occlusion, fine-grained components, and propagation of bad spatial priors are acknowledged rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The method relies heavily on closed or externally changing components, especially Nano Banana Pro/Gemini-style image editing and VLM feedback, as well as large 3D generators. This weakens reproducibility and makes it hard to disentangle the paper's contribution from the capabilities and quirks of proprietary foundation models.

The experimental protocol lacks important details. The human rating setup is underspecified, including the number of raters, instructions, randomization/blinding, inter-rater agreement, and whether raters saw paired or independent outputs. The VLM rating protocol is also under-described and may correlate with the same generative priors used by the system.

The baseline set is only partially convincing. Some baselines such as Jigsaw and 2BY2 are not designed for this exact open-ended text/image-conditioned composition setting, while a closer related method, Copy-Transform-Paste, is discussed but not included experimentally. This makes the size of the claimed advantage somewhat difficult to calibrate.

The dataset contribution needs more scrutiny. Since the dataset is generated through automated pipelines using proprietary models, the paper should better document filtering criteria, failure rates, asset provenance/licensing, physical-property annotations if any, and whether the poses are actually useful in downstream simulators or manipulation tasks.

The agentic refinement loop is promising but somewhat opaque. It is unclear how often it is invoked, how many iterations are typically needed, what prompts/templates are used, how failures are detected automatically, and how much cost/runtime it adds. The maximum of five iterations is reported, but practical efficiency statistics are missing.

The claims of being physically sound or suitable for robotic simulation are only partially supported. Collision metrics are useful, but the paper does not evaluate stability, contact realism, support relationships, center of mass, friction/material properties, articulation, or downstream manipulation performance.

The technical novelty is moderate. The paper combines strong existing generative models, PartField segmentation, GeoTransformer registration, ICP, SDF collision penalties, and VLM-based prompt refinement in an effective pipeline, but the individual algorithmic components are not deeply novel. The contribution is mainly in the integration and system framing.
The code and dataset availability statement appears incomplete in the manuscript text, which is a concern for a systems/dataset paper where release quality is central to impact.
